strengths: The paper proposes a simple, architecture-agnostic, plug-and-play inference-time guidance method (TAG) that requires no additional score/network evaluations, retraining, or external unconditional/conditional branch, making it computationally cheap relative to CFG-style residual scaling methods.

The geometric decomposition (radial/normal vs tangential component relative to the current iterate) is intuitive and is supported by a clear qualitative visualization (Figure 2) showing that the tangential component of the update carries most of the semantic structure.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple backbones (SD1.5, SD2.1, SDXL, SD3/flow-matching) and multiple existing guidance methods (SAG, PAG, SEG, CFG) in both unconditional (ImageNet) and conditional (MS-COCO) settings, consistently showing FID/IS/CLIPScore improvements at matched or reduced NFEs.

A first-order theoretical argument (Theorem 4.1) links tangential amplification to a monotonic increase in a local log-likelihood (Taylor) gain, giving some principled motivation beyond a purely heuristic trick.

The limitations section is honest, includes an analysis (eq. 21) of why excessive amplification causes over-smoothing/degradation, and proposes a concrete direction (adaptive/hyperparameter-free gains) for future work.
Reasonable reproducibility support: pseudocode (Algorithm 1-2) and actual implementation code snippets (Appendix B) using standard libraries (PyTorch, Diffusers) are provided.
weaknesses: The 'tangential/normal' decomposition is defined relative to the origin-centered radial direction of the current iterate x_k (P(x)=x x^T/||x||^2), which is a specific and somewhat ad hoc geometric choice; its correspondence to the true data manifold's tangent space (as opposed to simply the noise-schedule's iso-norm sphere) is asserted rather than rigorously justified, especially at high noise levels where x_k is dominated by Gaussian noise.

Theorem 4.1 only guarantees monotonic increase of a first-order (linearized) log-likelihood proxy, which is a fairly loose guarantee; the paper's own ablations (Table 1, Fig. 8a) show non-monotonic, and eventually degrading, FID/IS behavior as eta increases, indicating the first-order theoretical justification does not tightly predict practical behavior, and the explanation for the degradation (eq. 21) is offered post hoc rather than being part of a unified theoretical account.

Central claims about 'hallucination reduction' are not evaluated with any hallucination-specific metric (e.g., mode-interpolation quantification, structural/anatomical-plausibility checks, human evaluation); the paper instead relies on generic FID/IS/CLIPScore, which are only indirect proxies for hallucination.

The toy 2D branching-distribution experiment (Figure 3), which is the clearest controlled test of the mode-interpolation/OOD hypothesis, is presented only qualitatively; no quantitative distributional similarity metric (e.g., Wasserstein distance, likelihood under the true branch distribution) is reported to substantiate the claim that TAG 'achieves the highest similarity to the GT distribution.'

No direct quantitative comparison to the most closely related geometry-aware guidance methods explicitly discussed in the related work (e.g., Sadat et al. 2025, Kwon et al. 2025 TCFG), despite these being described as conceptually very similar (parallel/orthogonal decomposition of the guidance direction); this omission makes it hard to assess TAG's real incremental benefit over these prior works.

The optimal amplification factor eta appears to be sensitive to model/sampler/guidance combination (values range from 1.05 to 2.5 across tables) with no principled selection procedure beyond manual sweep/ablation, which limits out-of-the-box usability despite the plug-and-play claim.

Most quantitative tables lack variance/confidence intervals (only Table 4 reports ±), and results are based on a single run per configuration, making it hard to judge the statistical significance of the reported FID/IS gains, some of which are modest (e.g., SD2.1+TAG FID 100.977→88.788, single-digit relative IS changes in several rows).

strengths: The geometric decomposition of the sampling update into radial (normal) and tangential components via Tweedie's formula is a clean and intuitive idea, and the qualitative visualizations (Fig. 2, Fig. 3) make a reasonably convincing case that the tangential component carries semantic structure.

TAG is genuinely plug-and-play: it requires no retraining, no extra network evaluations, and composes with several existing guidance mechanisms (CFG, SAG, PAG, SEG), which is demonstrated across multiple backbones (SD1.5, SD2.1, SDXL, SD3) and both conditional/unconditional settings.

The paper provides a first-order theoretical argument (Theorem 4.1) connecting increased tangential amplification to a local log-likelihood gain, and it is commendably honest in the Limitations section about where this monotonicity prediction breaks down empirically (Eq. 21), rather than hiding the discrepancy.
Fairly broad empirical sweep (multiple guidance baselines, multiple backbones, an NFE-efficiency comparison, and a flow-matching backbone) showing consistent FID/IS improvements at matched compute.
weaknesses: The reported FID values for 'unconditional' Stable Diffusion generation (60-125, Tables 1-3, 5) are far outside the range typically reported for ImageNet generation in the literature (single digits to low tens for standard generators), suggesting the 'unconditional' setup (likely empty-prompt SD) is a non-standard and poorly justified evaluation protocol; this casts doubt on whether the reported gains are meaningful improvements in sample quality/hallucination or artifacts of an unusual evaluation regime not clearly explained or grounded against literature baselines.

The central theoretical claim (Theorem 4.1: monotonic increase of first-order gain with amplification η) is contradicted by the paper's own empirical results: FID as a function of η is non-monotonic (U-shaped, e.g., Table 1: 67.971 at η=1.05 vs. 71.801 at η=1.25; Fig. 8 ablation shows degradation at larger η). The theorem is only a local, first-order statement and the paper concedes in the Limitations section that higher-order effects dominate outside a narrow η range, which substantially weakens the practical value/predictive power of the 'proof' as support for the method's design.

No metric directly measures hallucination (e.g., object-existence/counting checks, human evaluation, or a hallucination-specific benchmark such as those used by Aithal et al. 2024, which motivates the paper). The paper relies entirely on FID/IS/CLIPScore as proxies, which are known to be imperfect surrogates for semantic correctness/hallucination, undermining the core claim of being 'hallucination-resistant.'

Missing direct empirical comparison to several closely related and recently cited methods that target the same tangential-mismatch phenomenon (e.g., Kwon et al. 2025 TCFG, Sadat et al. 2025, Dinh et al. 2025 Representative Guidance), despite these being discussed as directly motivating/competing approaches in the related work section. Without these comparisons it is hard to assess TAG's relative contribution.

Inconsistent evaluation protocols across tables (e.g., 30K samples for Table 1/3/5 vs. 10K for Table 2) and no reported variance/multiple seeds for FID/IS (only CLIPScore reports ± values), making it difficult to assess statistical significance of the (often modest) improvements.

The amplification hyperparameter η needs separate tuning per backbone/setting (1.05-1.3 range with different optimal values reported across tables), and no principled or automatic selection procedure is provided (deferred to future work), limiting practical usability as a 'plug-and-play' method as claimed.

There is an apparent inconsistency between the conditional TAG formulation described in the main text (Eqs. 19-20, Algorithm 2, defined via ε-space projections) and the pseudocode in Appendix B Algorithm 4, which operates in score space (s_u, s_c) with different projection operations (proj_par, q_aligned) not clearly matching the equations in Section 4.2; this raises reproducibility and clarity concerns.
The project page/code link referenced in the abstract footnote is left blank, and no public repository is provided, limiting independent reproducibility beyond the pseudocode in the appendix.

The 2D toy demonstration (Fig. 3) supporting the mode-interpolation narrative is purely qualitative with no quantitative distributional metric (e.g., Wasserstein distance to ground truth), weakening the evidentiary strength of this key motivating illustration.

strengths: The paper offers a genuinely novel geometric perspective on diffusion guidance: decomposing the update step into radial (normal) and tangential components relative to the current sample, and showing empirically (Fig. 2) that the tangential component carries most of the semantic content while the normal component is largely 'noise-like'.

TAG is architecture-agnostic, training-free, and adds negligible computational overhead (a projection and rescale after each solver step), making it easy to combine with existing sampling pipelines and guidance methods (CFG, SAG, PAG, SEG), as demonstrated in Tables 1 and 4.

The method is validated across a reasonably broad set of backbones and samplers (SD v1.5/2.1/XL/3, DDIM, DPM++), and consistently improves FID/IS at matched NFEs, and in several cases lets fewer NFEs match or beat more expensive baselines (Table 3).

A theoretical justification via a first-order Taylor expansion of the log-likelihood is provided, with a clean monotonicity proof (Theorem 4.1) and an explicit failure-mode analysis (Section 4.1/6) explaining why naively amplifying the normal component over-smooths images, which lends coherence to the method design.

The extension to conditional generation (C-TAG, Section 4.2) via conditional-unconditional tangent reconciliation is a sensible generalization and is empirically shown to improve CLIPScore/FID when layered on top of CFG/PAG/SEG (Table 4).

The synthetic 2D branching-distribution experiment (Fig. 3) provides an intuitive, controlled illustration of the claimed mechanism (reducing off-manifold/OOD mass) that is easier to interpret than pixel-space FID alone.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result (Theorem 4.1) approximates the true score by the model's own predicted noise ε_θ and then shows that amplifying the projection of ε_θ onto itself increases a 'gain' that is essentially ‖P⊥ε_θ‖² term (Eq. 29-30); this is close to a tautology (amplifying a vector along its own direction increases its self-inner-product) rather than a proof that image quality/likelihood under the *true* data density improves. The paper does not clearly distinguish the model-score approximation from genuine log-likelihood gain, so the theoretical guarantee is weaker than the framing suggests.

The reported FID values for baselines are unusually high for the backbones used (e.g., unconditional SD v1.5 DDIM FID ≈ 76.9, SD v2.1 ≈ 101, SDXL ≈ 124 in Tables 1-2), which suggests a non-standard/unfavorable evaluation setup (unconditional sampling from models trained primarily for conditional generation). This makes it unclear whether the relative FID improvements from TAG generalize to more standard/favorable evaluation protocols where baseline FID is already low.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported for FID/IS in the main tables (only IS has ± in Table 4, and no CLIPScore/FID variance anywhere), making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (often single-digit FID differences) are robust rather than run-to-run noise.

The useful range of the amplification hyperparameter η appears narrow and backbone/sampler-dependent (Fig. 8, Table 1), with quality degrading quickly for larger η; the paper acknowledges this as a limitation but does not provide a principled or automatic way to select η beyond manual/grid search per backbone, limiting practical plug-and-play claims.

Comparisons to some of the most closely related recent geometry-aware guidance baselines mentioned in the text (e.g., Kwon et al. 2025 TCFG, Sadat et al. 2025) are discussed conceptually but not included as quantitative baselines in the main tables, leaving open how TAG compares against these directly competing geometric approaches.

The reproducibility statement is minimal (only mentions PyTorch/Diffusers), without explicit hyperparameter tables, exact scheduler settings, or seed values, which could hinder exact replication despite the algorithmic pseudocode provided in the appendix.
